explanations.explanation: Mortally ill, and Hezekiah prays. The text says, “So he prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign.” (2 Chronicles 32:24) When my oven timer starts beeping in a weird way, I stand there and stare at it, and staring has never fixed one timer. Hezekiah took his problem to the right place.

Wanting a doctor when you're sick is as normal as wanting a cookie when you smell the oven. But these verses never mention physicians. The writer tells us that Hezekiah prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign (2 Chronicles 32:24).

A will is a sensible thing to write, but this passage doesn't mention one. What the text says is that Hezekiah became mortally ill, "So he prayed to the LORD…" (2 Chronicles 32:24). Prayer is the thing he does, and the LORD answers it.

That's right. Hezekiah prays, and the LORD "…spoke to him and gave him a sign." (2 Chronicles 32:24) The king is mortally ill, and he gets an answer. The text doesn't say here what the sign was, so I'm not going to make one up.

The text says the opposite. After Hezekiah prays, the LORD "…spoke to him and gave him a sign." (2 Chronicles 32:24) So the LORD answers him, and He gives a sign too. Don't let that little word False throw you, baker, it happens to the best of us.

The text puts it plainly: "But because his heart was proud, Hezekiah did not repay the favor shown to him." (2 Chronicles 32:25) Pride is the reason the writer gives. Pride is sneaky like that, because it can sit in a heart quietly and look like nothing.

Being busy is a great excuse, and I've used it on my own to-do list. But the text doesn't give it here. It says "…because his heart was proud, Hezekiah did not repay the favor shown to him." (2 Chronicles 32:25)

explanations.answer: His advisers talk him out of it
explanations.explanation: Advisers don't show up in this verse at all. The text gives one reason, and it's inside Hezekiah himself: "…because his heart was proud…" (2 Chronicles 32:25) No one has to push a proud heart. It manages fine on its own.

That's right. The verse says "…wrath came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem." (2 Chronicles 32:25) It comes upon the king and upon the whole land together. That's a heavy line, so I'm going to let it sit for a second.
The text says more than that. The wrath came "…upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem." (2 Chronicles 32:25) So Hezekiah is included, but he isn't alone. It's a heavy verse, baker.

The verse doesn't narrow it down to leaders. It says wrath "…came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem." (2 Chronicles 32:25) That means the king, the land and the city. It's a heavy moment, so I'm going to be gentle with it.

Yes, the text says, "Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart…" (2 Chronicles 32:26). Pride was the problem, and humbling is what he does about it. I've humbled myself in front of a burnt batch before, and it's a lot cheaper than pride.

Defending is a very human move when we're caught, and I've done it over a lopsided cookie. But the text says, "Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart…" (2 Chronicles 32:26). Humbled is the word the verse uses.
Hiding is a very human move, and I know it well. But the verse says, "Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart…" (2 Chronicles 32:26). Humbled is the word, not hid.

Not quite, baker. The text says, "Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart—he and the people of Jerusalem…" (2 Chronicles 32:26). So Hezekiah isn't doing it all alone. The people of Jerusalem humble themselves with him.

That's right, baker. The verse says, "Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart—he and the people of Jerusalem…" (2 Chronicles 32:26). The king and the people of Jerusalem both do the humbling. So the statement is false.

explanations.answer: It does not come in Hezekiah's days
explanations.explanation: That's right. The text says they humbled themselves "…so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah." (2 Chronicles 32:26) The humbling and the wrath not coming are right there in the same verse. I'd call that a very good trade.

explanations.answer: It comes on them all the same
explanations.explanation: The verse says otherwise. After they humbled themselves, "…the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah." (2 Chronicles 32:26) So in his days it doesn't come. Notice the words "…during the days of Hezekiah." because the verse is careful about that.

This verse doesn't say anything about Assyria. It says "…the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah." (2 Chronicles 32:26) The "them" is Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem. It's about the wrath not coming, not about it moving to someone else.

The text says the opposite. "And Hezekiah prospered in all that he did." (2 Chronicles 32:30) That's the whole of what he did, the building and the riches included. Most of us would take a year like that without asking questions.

That's right. The verse says, "And Hezekiah prospered in all that he did." (2 Chronicles 32:30) Prospered is the word the text gives for everything he did, the building and the riches included. Struggling in most of it doesn't fit with that. So the statement doesn't match what the verse says.

explanations.answer: The wonder that happened in the land
explanations.explanation: That's right. The ambassadors "…were sent to him to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land…" (2 Chronicles 32:31) That's what they came to ask about. The text doesn't spell out which wonder it means, so I'll leave it right there.

An army is a fair guess, and a visitor who sees my ovens always asks how many cookies they bake. But the verse doesn't mention an army. It says the ambassadors were sent "…to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land…" (2 Chronicles 32:31) They came asking about a wonder, not counting soldiers.

A treaty sounds like serious grown-up business, and I'd have bet on it too. But no treaty shows up in this verse. The text says the ambassadors came "…to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land…" (2 Chronicles 32:31) That's the only reason it gives for their visit.

That's right, baker. "…God left him alone to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart." (2 Chronicles 32:31) Test is the word the text uses. It also says what the test is for, which is all that was in Hezekiah's heart.

Protect sounds comforting, like a warm oven mitt. But the text says God left him alone "…to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart." (2 Chronicles 32:31) The verse says test, not protect.

Punish is a fair guess, because the passage does talk about wrath earlier. But look at what this verse says: God left him alone "…to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart." (2 Chronicles 32:31) A punishment is for something already done. This one is about finding out what's in his heart. It's like leaving a timer off and just watching what happens in the kitchen. The verse says test, so that's the word to stay with.

explanations.answer: In the upper tombs of David's descendants
explanations.explanation: That's right. Hezekiah "…was buried in the upper tombs of David’s descendants." (2 Chronicles 32:33) David was Israel's king, and these tombs belong to his descendants. Hezekiah is laid to rest in those tombs.

explanations.answer: In the garden of his own palace
explanations.explanation: The text puts him somewhere else. Hezekiah "…was buried in the upper tombs of David’s descendants." (2 Chronicles 32:33) No palace garden is mentioned. The burial place the text names is the upper tombs of David's descendants.

explanations.answer: In the cave of Machpelah at Hebron
explanations.explanation: The cave of Machpelah is a real burial place. It's where Abraham buried his wife Sarah (Genesis 23:19). But Hezekiah's burial is in a different place: "…the upper tombs of David’s descendants." (2 Chronicles 32:33)
That's right, baker. "All Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor at his death." (2 Chronicles 32:33) It says all Judah and the people of Jerusalem. That's a big farewell.

The text says it's true. "All Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor at his death." (2 Chronicles 32:33) Honor came from all Judah, and from the people of Jerusalem too. So True is the answer.

That's right. The passage ends with "…his son Manasseh reigned in his place." (2 Chronicles 32:33) Manasseh is Hezekiah's son, and he takes the throne. The story of Hezekiah's reign closes here, but the story of the kings of Judah keeps going.

Eliakim, a palace official, does show up in the Bible (Isaiah 36:3). But the text here says, "…his son Manasseh reigned in his place." (2 Chronicles 32:33) The throne goes to Hezekiah's son, not an official.
Shebna, a scribe, also shows up in the Bible (Isaiah 36:3). But he isn't the one who takes the throne here. The text says, "…his son Manasseh reigned in his place." (2 Chronicles 32:33)
